did-lost-schooling-widen-the-gap.sentence: The disadvantage gap index narrowed from 3.34 in 2010/11 to 2.91 in 2018/19, the last year before the pandemic. When it was next measured, in 2021/22, it was 3.23, up 11% on 2018/19, and it is 3.22 in 2025/26. That undoes 71% of the narrowing between 2010/11 and 2018/19. Persistent absence was 10.9% of pupils in 2018/19 and peaked at 22.5% in 2021/22; it is 18.1% in 2024/25. Neither series is measured identically either side of the pandemic: the disadvantage gap index (no KS2 tests 2020, 2021) and persistent absence (recording rules changed in 2020), so compare the before and after figures with care.

has-pay-kept-up-with-prices.sentence: Rebased to 2000 = 100, average pay reached 233 by 2025 and prices (CPIH) 188: average pay +133%, prices (CPIH) +88%. Average pay rose faster. Relative to 2000, average pay ended 24% ahead of prices (CPIH).

have-rents-outrun-pay.sentence: Rebased to 2015 = 100, private rents reached 145 by 2025 and average pay 151: private rents +45%, average pay +51%. Average pay rose faster. Relative to 2015, private rents ended 4% behind average pay, having been 8% behind at the widest, in 2022.

what-does-the-debt-cost-to-carry.sentence: In 1993 net debt was 29.7% of GDP and the interest on it cost 2.7% of GDP. By 2025 the debt was 94.2% of GDP, 3.2 times its 1993 share of the economy, but interest cost 4.3% — 1.6 times, and it peaked at 4.7% in 2022. The difference is the rate: interest ÷ debt, the effective rate the state pays, went from 8.9% in 1993 to a low of 2.1% in 2020, and is back to 4.6% in 2025. Interest and debt are both set against the size of the economy here, so rising prices and growth do not flatter or inflate either one.
what-does-the-debt-cost-to-carry.unit: % of GDP, and % of the debt
